title: Precise Quantum Chemistry calculations with few Slater Determinants

paper_content.abstract: Slater determinants have underpinned quantum chemistry for nearly a century, yet their full potential has remained challenging to exploit. In this work, we show that a variational wavefunction composed of a few hundred optimized non-orthogonal determinants can achieve energy accuracies comparable to the state of the art. This is obtained by introducing an optimization method that leverages the quadratic dependence of the variational energy on the orbitals of each determinant, enabling an exact iterative optimization, and uses an efficient tensor-contraction algorithm to evaluate the effective Hamiltonian with a computational cost that scales as the fourth power of the number of basis functions. We benchmark the accuracy of the proposed method with exact full-configuration interaction results where available, and we achieve lower variational energies than coupled cluster (CCSD(T)) for several molecules in the double-zeta basis.
paper_content.introduction:
Slater Determinants (SDs) have been instrumental in shaping our understanding of quantum chemistry since their introduction nearly a century ago. In 1927, Heitler and London [1] explained the qualitative nature of the covalent bond in H using a wave function composed of a sum of non-orthogonal SDs built from single-atom orbitals. About two decades later, Coulson and Fischer [2] demonstrated that the Heitler-London wave function could be significantly improved by allowing atomic orbitals to hybridize and variationally optimizing them, thereby eliminating the need to introduce ionic structures which appear unphysical for H . Subsequent developments along this line, most notably the introduction of the Generalized Valence Bond Ansatz [3] and the Spin-Coupled wave function [4, 5], marked the foundation of modern Valence Bond theory [6, 7], and played a key role in our current understanding of chemical bonding. In Valence Bond theory, bonds emerge from resonating chemical structures, which are superpositions of basic wavefunctions and are themselves spin-determined linear combinations of non-orthogonal SDs constructed with semi-localized orbitals. The compactness of the wave function is crucial for this interpretation and can only be achieved through simultaneous optimization of both the structures and the orbitals. However, this remains a challenging task compared to molecular orbital based methods [8], which exploit orbital orthogonality to achieve unmatched numerical efficiency, at the expense of interpretability. Achieving chemical accuracy requires too many contributing SDs when built with orthogonal orbitals, while non-orthogonal SDs, potentially more interpretable, pose significant numerical challenges when high accuracy is required.

In view of the above, it is not surprising that many techniques have been proposed to optimize SDs. The Full Configuration Interaction (FCI) expansion, while exact within a chosen finite basis, scales exponentially with basis-set size, rendering it impractical for all but the very smallest systems. Approximate methods can be generally divided into two classes: (i) methods using one or multiple fixed-reference determinants that optimize a linear combination of excitations thereof, and (ii) multi-configuration determinantal methods that optimize the orbitals of the SDs, along with the configuration interaction (CI) coefficients.

A notable example of a method belonging to the first category is truncated CI, where excitations from a reference determinant are limited to a certain excitation level. For instance, only single and double excitations are included in CISD. In such cases, the number of determinants is combinatorial in the excitation level and CI truncation breaks size-consistency. The prohibitive scaling can be mitigated by selected-CI methods, which retain only a subset of relevant excitations. However, identifying the important determinants is generally a nontrivial task. Quadratic Configuration Interaction [9] and Coupled Cluster [10] methods such as CCSD(T) correct the size-consistency by approximately including also higher excitations; however, unlike CI methods, they are non-variational and come at an increased computational cost. The methods discussed so far all use orthogonal Slater determinants. The non-orthogonal configuration interaction technique [11], on the other hand, optimizes a linear combination of given, fixed, non-orthogonal Slater Determinants.

The second class of methods, which is the most relevant in spirit to the topic of this article, consists of a variety of multi-configurational approaches that employ different strategies to optimize both the CI coefficients and the orbitals of the SDs. Thanks to the improved quality of the SDs achieved with the orbital optimization, these CI expansions are typically much more compact than those in the first class, albeit at the cost of increased computational effort. Multi-configurational self-consistent field methods, such as the Complete Active Space Self Consistent Field Method [12], optimize a single orbital rotation applied to all or a subset of the CI determinants, and have recently been generalized to non-orthogonal orbitals [13]. Gradient-based approaches optimizing only the orbitals of a single determinant at a time have been proposed for two determinants [14], and many determinants [15], or Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov wavefunctions [16, 17]. Resonating Hartree-Fock [18–20] and nonorthogonal multiconfigurational self-consistent field [21] exploit the Thouless parametrization of the SDs [22] to optimize all orbitals simultaneously using gradient-based methods. However, it can be difficult to make the process converge [17, 23, 24]. Valence Bond Self-Consistent Field methods [25, 26] use second-order optimizers to optimize a sum of non-orthogonal determinants. Multi-configuration time-dependent Hartree methods [27], extended to fermions [28] use numerical integration to apply the real or imaginary time evolution to the determinants.

SDs also play a crucial role in many-body methods such as Quantum Monte Carlo. Compact SD expansions serve as efficient trial wavefunctions in Auxiliary-Field Quantum Monte Carlo [29, 30] and Diffusion Monte Carlo [31], and underpin variational ansätze like the Slater-Jastrow form [32] as well as recent variants augmented with neural networks [33–36].

In this work we show that a sum of fewer than a thousand SDs is sufficient to accurately represent the all-electron ground-state wavefunction of small-size molecules, when the SDs are fully optimized without orthogonality constraints. These results are achieved with a computational optimization technique that we introduce in this article, which we call the Exact Iterative Determinant-Orbital Solver (EIDOS). EIDOS iteratively optimizes the variational energy when viewed as a function of a string of orbitals, by selecting one orbital from each determinant and solving a generalized eigenvalue problem at every step. It relies on: (i) the direct parameterization of the molecular orbital coefficients, as opposed to the popular Thouless parameterization of the SDs [22]; (ii) an efficient analytical evaluation of the Hessian of the energy functional, resulting in a favorable O(m4) scaling with the basis set size m (see the Methods Section for details). We assess the accuracy of EIDOS on several molecules in the cc-pVDZ basis, benchmarking with full-CI data where available, and with DMRG and coupled-cluster (CCSD(T)) otherwise. We find that our variational energies are consistently below coupled-cluster, and within chemical accuracy of full-CI and DMRG, demonstrating that EIDOS is competitive with state-of-the-art methods, but with significantly more favorable scaling. We additionally discuss how the number of determinants scales with bond order, and we demonstrate convergence toward the complete-basis-set limit for LiH. To test the method’s robustness, we analyze the strongly-correlated regime along the N dissociation curve, and we verify that it correctly reproduces the triplet ground state of O .

where N is the number of determinants, | 0 ⟩ is the vacuum state, and

SΦˆ(I,σ) := (cid:89) nσ i=1 (cid:88) m µ=1 ϕ(I,σ) i,µ cˆ† µ,σ , (2)

where ϕ(I,σ) are independent orbitals, n is the number of electrons of spin σ, m is the number of basis orbitals, and cˆ† is the creation operator of an electron in basis orbital µ with spin σ.

We optimize the average energy of the non-orthogonal Slater determinant wave-function ansatz of Eq. (1) using our novel EIDOS algorithm. Below, we briefly outline the main ideas underlying EIDOS, and refer the reader to the Methods section for the details. The efficiency of EIDOS relies on two key aspects: (i) the average energy of the wavefunction of Eq. (1) is the ratio of two quadratic functions of ϕ(1,σ),...,ϕ(ND,σ) at fixed electron label i = 1, which implies that these parameters can be optimized by solving a series of generalized eigenvalue problems, where the procedure is repeated after a random quantum-state-preserving electron-label transformation in each determinant; (ii) the needed effective quadratic forms can be computed with a total computational cost of O(m4) with an efficient tensor-contraction strategy.

Benchmark with CCSD(T), DMRG and FCI for equilibrium geometries in the cc-pVDZ basis. To validate the accuracy of the proposed EIDOS method, we compare it against CCSD(T), and, where available, DMRG and FCI, for the all-electron ground-state energy of several molecules at equilibrium in the cc-pVDZ basis set. In our calculations, the electron number varies from 4 (LiH) to 20 (for LiCl), except for the Krypton atom with 36 electrons in 27 orbitals, where we perform a particle-hole transformation to reduce the effective number of interacting particles to 18. As reported in Fig. 1, the EIDOS optimized energies from up to N = 768 Slater determinants (N = 2048 is obtained with the extension described in Supplementary Note 3) are well within chemical accuracy (1 kcal/mol) with respect to FCI, including those at the limit of what is still tractable by current distributed FCI codes [37]. Furthermore, our variational energies are consistently lower than those obtained using the coupled cluster method at the CCSD(T) level. The latter is considered the gold standard for molecules near equilibrium with minimal multireference character, where dynamic electron correlation dominates, which is the case for a large part of the molecules we consider here. These results are significant because CCSD(T) has an asymptotic computational scaling of O(m7), while our method scales like O(m4).

For all molecules we find the expected spin symmetry for the ground state, with a maximal spin contamination at 768 determinants of ⟨ Sˆ2 ⟩ S(S+1) 5 10−3 ( 9 10−4 with 2048 determinants) for BN, and less for the other molecules. We also note that 768 determinants consistently improve the results of 512 determinants, and that the optimization steps of the EIDOS algorithm to achieve convergence are roughly independent of the number of determinants (see Supplementary Note 1).

Scaling of the number of SDs with bond order. In general, we expect the number of SDs needed to precisely model the ground state to increase with correlations and, in particular, we expect a dependence on the number of valence electrons. To verify this picture in a controlled setting, we consider the three molecules LiF, BeO and N , which all have a similar number of electrons, n 12,14 , the same number of basis orbitals in the cc-pVDZ basis set, m = 28, but different bond order. In Fig. 2 we report the EIDOS energy error w.r.t. FCI as a function of the number of determinants, ranging from N = 1 up to N = 768, observing a smooth and consistent scaling. Moreover, the log-log scale we use in the plot graphically shows that the decay of the energy error is certainly not slower than a power-law of the inverse number of SDs. The slope of the decay clearly decreases with the bond order/number of valence electrons, meaning that for N we need more than an order of magnitude more determinants to attain chemical accuracy than what is needed for LiF, with BeO lying in between. The single-bonded BH shows a similar scaling as LiF, while it is interesting to remark that the curves for C and BN, which are considered to be doubly-bonded molecules, nearly collapse on the curve of the triple-bonded N .

Convergence to the large-basis-set limit. In Fig. 3 we consider the ground-state energy of the LiH molecule at equilibrium distance obtained with the EIDOS technique for various basis sets of sizes ranging from m = 6 to m=146 orbitals, the largest for which FCI energies are still available [37]. The approximate curve collapse for the energy error in a given basis set as a function of the ratio of the basis set size m and the number of SDs (shown in the inset of Fig. 3) suggests that the number of determinants needed to get a fixed error in a given basis scales linearly with the basis set size. We conjecture that this might be due to the short-distance cusp conditions of the continuum-space wave function, which require having an increasing number of determinants in the approach to the continuum limit. Nevertheless, as we show in the main plot of Fig. 3, the absolute energy decreases with increasing basis set size m for a fixed number of SDs N , as does the error with respect to the true ground-state energy in the infinite-basis-set limit.

Capturing static correlations. As a prototypical example of bond breaking, we consider the Nitrogen molecule. As its bond is stretched, the wavefunction acquires an inherent multireference character. Single-reference methods such as CISD and CCSD(T) have serious difficulties there, converging more slowly or not converging at all [38]. In Fig. 4 we show the EIDOS dissociation curve of the N molecule in comparison to UCISD (which uses 30724 orthogonal determinants), UCCSD(T) and DMRG. We outperform UCISD and UCCSD(T) already with a few hundred independent Slater determinants. As can be seen in the inset, close to equilibrium, we obtain energies within chemical accuracy from DMRG, while deviations become larger at extended bond lengths, where static-correlation effects emerge. These effects are, however, less severe than in CCSD, which inherits them from the UHF reference, and we do not rule out that they could be further alleviated with an appropriate choice of the initial guess.

Triplet and singlet dioxygen states. As an additional application, we discuss the low-energy states of molecular oxygen for different sectors of the M and S quantum numbers. While ⟨ Sˆ2 ⟩ is directly tuned to the value of S in this calculation, we can optionally add a λSˆ2 penalty term to the Hamiltonian at no extra cost during the optimization. In Fig. 5 we study the convergence of the EIDOS method to the O ground state, both in the M =0 and M =1 spin sectors, which is found to be a triplet in both sectors, as expected. For the M =1 sector we need fewer determinants to accurately represent the wavefunction due to the smaller size of the subspace. By adding a λSˆ2 penalty term, with λ = 0.1, we can converge to a singlet excited state. The inset of Fig. 5 shows the absence of spin contamination, apart from the lowest number of determinants in the M =0 sector.

The Exact Iterative Determinant-Orbital Solver (EIDOS). In this section, we present our method to variationally optimize the average energy of an ansatz consisting of a sum of SDs by solving at each step a linear algebra problem. We first show why it is enough to solve a generalized eigenvalue problem, and afterwards how to efficiently compute the terms appearing in the linear algebra problem.

Our first finding is that the energy expectation value with the wave-function ansatz of Eq. (3), when regarded as a function of a single orbital of each SD, is simply a ratio of two quadratic forms

E = ⟨ Φ¯ | Hˆ | Φ¯ ⟩ / ⟨ Φ¯ | Φ¯ ⟩ = v† H v / v† S v , (7)

where v ∈ C(ND×m), defined by

v Iµ := ϕ(I) 1,µ , (8)

is the “vector” with flattened index Iµ, for I ∈ { 1,...,N } and µ ∈ { 1,...,m } , containing the orbitals that were factored out from each determinant, and H , S ∈ C(ND×m)×(ND×m) are the “effective matrices” for respectively the Hamiltonian and the norm of the wave-function, and they are given by

H Iµ,Jν = ⟨ Φ(I) 1+ | cˆ µ Hˆcˆ† ν | Φ(J) 1+ ⟩ , (9)

S Iµ,Jν = ⟨ Φ(I) 1+ | cˆ µ cˆ† ν | Φ(J) 1+ ⟩ , (10)

where I,J ∈ { 1,...,N } and µ,ν ∈ { 1,...,m } . The hole-wavefunction matrix elements ⟨ Φ(I) 1+ | cˆ µ Hˆcˆ† ν | Φ(J) 1+ ⟩ needed for H can be calculated in a numerically-exact way at an asymptotic cost of O(N2 m 4 ), including the singular case where the hole-SDs are linearly dependent. Similarly, ⟨ Φ(I) 1+ | cˆ µ cˆ† ν | Φ(J) 1+ ⟩ can be calculated at a cost of O(N2 m 2 ). Therefore, asymptotically, calculating H is not more expensive than the energy expectation value.

The energy Eq. (7) takes the form of a generalized Rayleigh quotient, and can be minimized exactly w.r.t. v by solving the generalized eigenvalue problem (GEV)

H v = ϵ S v , (11)

with a computational cost of O(N D 3m3) operations. We remark that S is singular, with null space spanned by the orbitals of the hole-SDs | Φ(I) 1+ ⟩ . By projecting out the kernel of S , the problem can be reduced from N D m to a smaller eigenvalue problem of size N D (m n+1).

The procedure described so far minimizes the energy with respect to a single orbital of each SD. The simplest algorithm that one can devise is an iterative one, where one selects a different orbital at every step. After optimizing an orbital, the wavefunction reaches a local minimum with respect to the coefficients of this orbital. However, as soon as another orbital is optimized, this is in general no longer true for the previously optimized one, requiring re-optimization of all orbitals until a stationary point is reached. The selection of orbitals for this can be done deterministically through sweeps, or stochastically by independently selecting the orbitals of each determinant in e.g. a uniform way. Here we consider a more general stochastic approach where a random linear combination of the orbitals of the previous step is optimized. The SD representation ( ϕ(I) 1 , ϕ(I) 2 ,..., ϕ(I) n ) in Eq. (4) is not unique, and the different redundant representations are related through the special linear group SL(n,C), i.e. the group of square matrices with determinant 1. We can make use of this by stochastically sampling V(I) ∈ SL(n,C) independently for each determinant I and transforming the orbitals as

ϕ(I) i (cid:55)→ (cid:88) n j=1 V(I) ij ϕ(I) j , (12)

which leaves the quantum state unchanged. Simple sweeps and uniform selection are included as special cases. The complete iterative algorithm is sketched in Box 1.

We discuss an efficient generalization for the case when the wavefunction is an eigenstate of Sˆ z (Eq. (1) in the main text) in Supplementary Note 2. For a single determinant this is equivalent to an unrestricted Hartree-Fock calculation. We remark that the method cannot be used to optimize a restricted Ansatz (Φˆ(I↑) ≡ Φˆ(I↓)), since the resulting wave function is not multilinear. In Supplementary Note 3 we discuss an extension of the method to reduce the size of the eigenvalue problem based on the selective optimization of orbitals of only a subset of all determinants at every step, which is used to obtain the 2048-determinant results of Fig. 1.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The authors introduce their EIDOS method, a (as far as I know) novel algorithm for variational optimization of non-orthogonal Slater determinant expansions, variationally optimizing both the orbitals and CI amplitudes simultaneously in a greedy quasi-randomized approach. They demonstrate that using a few hundred such fully optimized determinants yields ground-state energies for small molecules with accuracy rivalling or surpassing standard methods (e.g., CCSD(T)), at a polynomial computational cost (for a fixed determinant number). The history of non-orthogonal CI expansions is long, and there have been many approaches suggested previously. The high accuracy of these expansions for small molecules is well known, although they are largely niche approaches due to the lack of size extensivity and (exponential?) scaling with number of determinants.
The main success of the work to be celebrated is the development of the algorithm for a full quasi-randomized variational optimization of the orbitals of the determinants. It is a neat approach which linearizes the determinants based on random rotations of the variations of a single degree of freedom. This is a significant achievement, and the ideas of this optimization approach could find broader impact.
However, the results are only presented up to a maximum of 20 electrons, and while accurate, does not currently enable calculations which cannot be achieved with alternate state of the art methods (e.g. DMRG or selected-CI). This is a high bar for the initial introduction of a new algorithm, and would still be happy to see it published as a novel algorithm, but with some more results detailing the scope of systems which the method could treat, and a wider discussion about the scaling of the algorithm with system size. In particular, while the lack of size consistency is noted, this major limitation (and the related lack of size extensivity) is largely glossed over. I would suggest this needs further scrutiny for a more honest appraisal of the potential of the method and its prospects. While the SI has a plot of size consistency for dissociated N2, more instructive would be the scaling of the error with respect to system size (i.e. characterizing the size extensivity error) – do we expect to require an exponential number of determinants for fixed relative error? A formal exponential number of determinants is not a disqualifying characteristic either (see e.g. DMRG and sCI) – if this has a small prefactor/exponent, then this can still be a useful method, and at least clarify the domain of applicability of this tool.
I would suggest e.g. a series of increasing length chain of Hydrogen atoms at a fixed interatomic spacing, and to observe the error compared to DMRG for fixed determinant number as additional plots in the main text (and at changing bond lengths). Presumably the correlation energy will converge to zero, but at what rate? How does this compare to CISD or CCSD (the latter being size extensive)? How does the number of determinants need to scale to counteract this? This would be more instructive than the bond order or basis set plots, the latter of which in particular is not expected to scale exponentially. This plot may also clarify the potential of the approach to extend to results beyond what is possible with DMRG or other systematically improvable methods, even if not possible with the current implementation.
Other recommended changes:
- Fig. 1 should compare results to DMRG rather than CCSD(T). All systems presented should be able to be solved essentially exactly with DMRG, and so would make a far better reference.
- Only a couple of sentences are given in the main text (not in the methods section) to describe the algorithm, and this is rather opaque. The methods section is good for describing the technical details, but given that the algorithm itself is the main novelty of the approach and major scientific advance, I would hope for a little more in the main text to describe it qualitatively.
- Furthermore, it would be good to have more insights into the convergence of the algorithm, especially in tricky cases. For instance, this is a quasi-randomized greedy optimization for a non-convex optimization problem (characterized as ‘partial-but-exact’ in the main text, which I found particularly uninformative!), so presumably there are cases where it finds local minima, exhibits a slow-down in convergence, or is found particularly sensitive to the initial conditions (perhaps e.g. where there are low-lying excited states?). It would be good to include some further insights into the numerical performance of the algorithm beyond Fig. B1, also commenting on the rate of convergence for different cases and starting point (e.g. keep the same random rotations, but reorder the initial orbitals?). How does this also vary with system size? Where is this algorithm expected to struggle to optimize to the true solutions compared to alternate iterative methods – are there any insights here?
- It would be good to compare the approach to modern approaches to (generalized) non-orthogonal CI, or fragment-localized optimization algorithms.
- There are a few minor typographical errors and inconsistent notation (e.g., missing or mismatched parentheses and indices) remain in the text—careful proofreading is advised.
Overall, the manuscript introduces an interesting and innovative algorithm for optimizing NOCI expansions. However, it does not clearly demonstrate, either numerically or a theoretical path, towards how the approach can be extended to larger systems or achieve higher accuracy (either in absolute terms or as a function of wall time) compared to existing alternatives. I would be pleased to see this work published in Nature Communications if these points can be addressed. Specifically, a more thorough and candid assessment of the algorithm’s scaling with system size is needed, both in terms of computational cost and accuracy with respect to number of determinants. This will help clarify the potential niche and practical applicability of this method, and justify its relevance for publication in a broad-interest scientific journal.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The concept of releasing the orthogonality restrictions to obtain more compact wave functions is a very attractive one and has received quite some attention over the last decade. In the here presented manuscript, a method is described that efficiently optimizes a wave function expressed as a linear combination of non-orthogonal Slater determinants. The method has the potential to be ground-breaking and the article can become a landmark paper in the field. There are a few things that need to be looked at to put the paper in the context of previous work (point 1); to discuss the stability of the algorithm when larger, more realistic systems are targeted (point 2); to get a feeling of how important non-orthogonality is (point 3); to address the importance of full orbital relaxation (point 4) and to clarify the way in which the orbitals are picked for optimization (point 5).
1. A comparison with the work of Olsen is in place (JCP 143, 114102). In this study (and some follow-up papers) a procedure is described in which the wave function is optimized with respect to both the CI and orbital coefficients in which the configuration state functions are expressed in non-orthogonal orbitals.
2. The use of iterative solvers seems to be an unavoidable step to surpass the memory bottleneck. Although not further worked out in the manuscript, this can be a critical step in the further development of the method and make it capable to use for other than the model molecules discussed here. With the increased number of degrees of freedoms due to the loss of orthogonality and the possible linear dependencies, the use of iterative solvers may degradate the stability of the optimization process. More information on the prospects of iterative solvers could be very helpful for other researchers in the field to judge the suitability of further developing this promising method.
3. What is the degree of non-orthogonality among the different determinants? Maximum overlap, percentage of (nearly) orthogonal determinants, to name a few indicators. An overview of some numerics on this point is more than welcome.
4. The method minimizes the average energy of the wave function expressed as a linear combination of non-orthogonal Slater Determinants. This is different than the approaches that adopt a "different orbitals for different electronic configurations" strategy. The latter includes full orbital relaxation for each electronic configuration (configuration state function, Slater determinant) in the wave function, while the here presented EIDOS variant only partially recovers orbital relaxation. This is especially relevant for core-hole states or for electronic states where charge transfer excitations contribute considerably to the wave function. In such cases a much larger number of SD will be needed to obtain a balanced description of the different configurations. Is is possible to design a strategy to perform independent optimizations of the most important electronic configurations and subsequently account for the interaction between these fully relaxed (non-orthogonal) states?
5. What is the reason to randomly select the orbital that is singled out for optimization? Does this imply special advantages compared to a simple linear selection procedure? How can we be sure that all orbitals in the SD are at least optimized once? Isn't this procedure prone to get stuck in a local minimum? Furthermore, it is not at all clear how steep will be the increase in the number of iterations in this loop when bigger systems (with much more occupied orbitals) are studied.

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Slater determinants have underpinned quantum chemistry for nearly a century, yet their full potential has remained challenging to exploit. In this work, we show that a variational wavefunction composed of a few hundred optimized non-orthogonal determinants can achieve energy accuracies comparable to the state of the art. This is obtained by introducing an optimization method that leverages the quadratic dependence of the variational energy on the orbitals of each determinant, enabling an exact iterative optimization, and uses an efficient tensor-contraction algorithm to evaluate the effective Hamiltonian with a computational cost that scales as the fourth power of the number of basis functions. We benchmark the accuracy of the proposed method with exact full-configuration interaction results where available, and we achieve lower variational energies than coupled cluster (CCSD(T)) for several molecules in the double-zeta basis.

---

## Introduction

Slater Determinants (SDs) have been instrumental in shaping our understanding of quantum chemistry since their introduction nearly a century ago. In 1927, Heitler and London [1] explained the qualitative nature of the covalent bond in H using a wave function composed of a sum of non-orthogonal SDs built from single-atom orbitals. About two decades later, Coulson and Fischer [2] demonstrated that the Heitler-London wave function could be significantly improved by allowing atomic orbitals to hybridize and variationally optimizing them, thereby eliminating the need to introduce ionic structures which appear unphysical for H . Subsequent developments along this line, most notably the introduction of the Generalized Valence Bond Ansatz [3] and the Spin-Coupled wave function [4, 5], marked the foundation of modern Valence Bond theory [6, 7], and played a key role in our current understanding of chemical bonding. In Valence Bond theory, bonds emerge from resonating chemical structures, which are superpositions of basic wavefunctions and are themselves spin-determined linear combinations of non-orthogonal SDs constructed with semi-localized orbitals. The compactness of the wave function is crucial for this interpretation and can only be achieved through simultaneous optimization of both the structures and the orbitals. However, this remains a challenging task compared to molecular orbital based methods [8], which exploit orbital orthogonality to achieve unmatched numerical efficiency, at the expense of interpretability. Achieving chemical accuracy requires too many contributing SDs when built with orthogonal orbitals, while non-orthogonal SDs, potentially more interpretable, pose significant numerical challenges when high accuracy is required.

In view of the above, it is not surprising that many techniques have been proposed to optimize SDs. The Full Configuration Interaction (FCI) expansion, while exact within a chosen finite basis, scales exponentially with basis-set size, rendering it impractical for all but the very smallest systems. Approximate methods can be generally divided into two classes: (i) methods using one or multiple fixed-reference determinants that optimize a linear combination of excitations thereof, and (ii) multi-configuration determinantal methods that optimize the orbitals of the SDs, along with the configuration interaction (CI) coefficients.

A notable example of a method belonging to the first category is truncated CI, where excitations from a reference determinant are limited to a certain excitation level. For instance, only single and double excitations are included in CISD. In such cases, the number of determinants is combinatorial in the excitation level and CI truncation breaks size-consistency. The prohibitive scaling can be mitigated by selected-CI methods, which retain only a subset of relevant excitations. However, identifying the important determinants is generally a nontrivial task. Quadratic Configuration Interaction [9] and Coupled Cluster [10] methods such as CCSD(T) correct the size-consistency by approximately including also higher excitations; however, unlike CI methods, they are non-variational and come at an increased computational cost. The methods discussed so far all use orthogonal Slater determinants. The non-orthogonal configuration interaction technique [11], on the other hand, optimizes a linear combination of given, fixed, non-orthogonal Slater Determinants.

The second class of methods, which is the most relevant in spirit to the topic of this article, consists of a variety of multi-configurational approaches that employ different strategies to optimize both the CI coefficients and the orbitals of the SDs. Thanks to the improved quality of the SDs achieved with the orbital optimization, these CI expansions are typically much more compact than those in the first class, albeit at the cost of increased computational effort. Multi-configurational self-consistent field methods, such as the Complete Active Space Self Consistent Field Method [12], optimize a single orbital rotation applied to all or a subset of the CI determinants, and have recently been generalized to non-orthogonal orbitals [13]. Gradient-based approaches optimizing only the orbitals of a single determinant at a time have been proposed for two determinants [14], and many determinants [15], or Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov wavefunctions [16, 17]. Resonating Hartree-Fock [18–20] and nonorthogonal multiconfigurational self-consistent field [21] exploit the Thouless parametrization of the SDs [22] to optimize all orbitals simultaneously using gradient-based methods. However, it can be difficult to make the process converge [17, 23, 24]. Valence Bond Self-Consistent Field methods [25, 26] use second-order optimizers to optimize a sum of non-orthogonal determinants. Multi-configuration time-dependent Hartree methods [27], extended to fermions [28] use numerical integration to apply the real or imaginary time evolution to the determinants.

SDs also play a crucial role in many-body methods such as Quantum Monte Carlo. Compact SD expansions serve as efficient trial wavefunctions in Auxiliary-Field Quantum Monte Carlo [29, 30] and Diffusion Monte Carlo [31], and underpin variational ansätze like the Slater-Jastrow form [32] as well as recent variants augmented with neural networks [33–36].

In this work we show that a sum of fewer than a thousand SDs is sufficient to accurately represent the all-electron ground-state wavefunction of small-size molecules, when the SDs are fully optimized without orthogonality constraints. These results are achieved with a computational optimization technique that we introduce in this article, which we call the Exact Iterative Determinant-Orbital Solver (EIDOS). EIDOS iteratively optimizes the variational energy when viewed as a function of a string of orbitals, by selecting one orbital from each determinant and solving a generalized eigenvalue problem at every step. It relies on: (i) the direct parameterization of the molecular orbital coefficients, as opposed to the popular Thouless parameterization of the SDs [22]; (ii) an efficient analytical evaluation of the Hessian of the energy functional, resulting in a favorable O(m4) scaling with the basis set size m (see the Methods Section for details). We assess the accuracy of EIDOS on several molecules in the cc-pVDZ basis, benchmarking with full-CI data where available, and with DMRG and coupled-cluster (CCSD(T)) otherwise. We find that our variational energies are consistently below coupled-cluster, and within chemical accuracy of full-CI and DMRG, demonstrating that EIDOS is competitive with state-of-the-art methods, but with significantly more favorable scaling. We additionally discuss how the number of determinants scales with bond order, and we demonstrate convergence toward the complete-basis-set limit for LiH. To test the method’s robustness, we analyze the strongly-correlated regime along the N dissociation curve, and we verify that it correctly reproduces the triplet ground state of O .

### Reviewer 1

The manuscript «Precise Quantum Chemistry calculations with few Slater Determinants» presents a variational wave function composed of nonorthogonal determinants which can compactly represent electron correlation effects. In general, I think the use of nonorthogonal Slater determinants is interesting, given that several previous works also indicates that nonorthogonal determinants can provide compact representations of the wave function. The code accompanying the paper was nicely set up and easy to use. However, I have some general and specific remarks regarding the paper.
General remarks:
1) The idea of using nonorthogonal determinants is not new, as also indicated by the authors since they cite some of the literature. Except that the authors seem to have an efficient implementation, I can’t see that this approach offers something that the other methods do not offer. If so, I think this needs to be adressed more clearly in the paper.
2) Although the boundary between dynamic and static correlation is a little bit blurry (especially along a dissociation curve) it is difficult to assess to which extent it captures static and/or dynamic correlation. In particular, in Fig 1 everything is compared to CCSD(T), indicating that it is dynamical correlation which is the target, since CCSD(T) is not suitable for static correlation. For some of the molecules in Fig 1, the results are closer to CCSD(T) than DMRG and FCI. However, the paper only talks about static correlation.
3) With respect to static correlation, I don’t understand why CCSD(T) (as highlighted in the abstract and discussion) is used as a reference for comparison, It is well known that low order truncations of CC are only suitable for capturing dynamical correlation and is not suitable for bond breaking (static correlation). Hence, since «Capturing static correlations» is mentioned explicitly, using CCSD(T) as a reference is the wrong choice. CCSD(T) contain dynamical correlation, which is not suitable for the stretching of the bond whereas DMRG only contain static correlation. Hence, for Fig 4, when the error wrt DMRG is already at milliHartree level (Nsd=768) that is just the error in the static correlation, and it does not include the dynamical correlation error (which I suppose can be large for stretching such an electron rich bond).
Specific remarks:
1) The random rotation of the orbitals: Is it correct to assume that there is no initial guess of the determinants, since the orbitals are randomly rotated? And since it is called a rotation, I suppose the transformation matrix in eq 12 is unitary. If so, this should be specified clearly. Also, I cannot find it clearly explained why one does the random rotation of the orbitals, and the magnitude of such a rotation (given it is unitary, there is some in the rotations). Further, given that nonorthogonal orbitals are used, the metric of the start guess orbitals is relevant. If the transformation matrix is unitary, the metric is will be conserved.
2) The molecular orbitals: I am not sure why the authors use quotation marks when writing molecular orbitals. As far as I can see, they are just normal nonorthogonal molecular orbitals (unless I am mistaken?), and there is no need for the use of quotation marks. ### Reviewer 2

The authors introduce their EIDOS method, a (as far as I know) novel algorithm for variational optimization of non-orthogonal Slater determinant expansions, variationally optimizing both the orbitals and CI amplitudes simultaneously in a greedy quasi-randomized approach. They demonstrate that using a few hundred such fully optimized determinants yields ground-state energies for small molecules with accuracy rivalling or surpassing standard methods (e.g., CCSD(T)), at a polynomial computational cost (for a fixed determinant number). The history of non-orthogonal CI expansions is long, and there have been many approaches suggested previously. The high accuracy of these expansions for small molecules is well known, although they are largely niche approaches due to the lack of size extensivity and (exponential?) scaling with number of determinants.
The main success of the work to be celebrated is the development of the algorithm for a full quasi-randomized variational optimization of the orbitals of the determinants. It is a neat approach which linearizes the determinants based on random rotations of the variations of a single degree of freedom. This is a significant achievement, and the ideas of this optimization approach could find broader impact.
However, the results are only presented up to a maximum of 20 electrons, and while accurate, does not currently enable calculations which cannot be achieved with alternate state of the art methods (e.g. DMRG or selected-CI). This is a high bar for the initial introduction of a new algorithm, and would still be happy to see it published as a novel algorithm, but with some more results detailing the scope of systems which the method could treat, and a wider discussion about the scaling of the algorithm with system size. In particular, while the lack of size consistency is noted, this major limitation (and the related lack of size extensivity) is largely glossed over. I would suggest this needs further scrutiny for a more honest appraisal of the potential of the method and its prospects. While the SI has a plot of size consistency for dissociated N2, more instructive would be the scaling of the error with respect to system size (i.e. characterizing the size extensivity error) – do we expect to require an exponential number of determinants for fixed relative error? A formal exponential number of determinants is not a disqualifying characteristic either (see e.g. DMRG and sCI) – if this has a small prefactor/exponent, then this can still be a useful method, and at least clarify the domain of applicability of this tool.
I would suggest e.g. a series of increasing length chain of Hydrogen atoms at a fixed interatomic spacing, and to observe the error compared to DMRG for fixed determinant number as additional plots in the main text (and at changing bond lengths). Presumably the correlation energy will converge to zero, but at what rate? How does this compare to CISD or CCSD (the latter being size extensive)? How does the number of determinants need to scale to counteract this? This would be more instructive than the bond order or basis set plots, the latter of which in particular is not expected to scale exponentially. This plot may also clarify the potential of the approach to extend to results beyond what is possible with DMRG or other systematically improvable methods, even if not possible with the current implementation.
Other recommended changes:
- Fig. 1 should compare results to DMRG rather than CCSD(T). All systems presented should be able to be solved essentially exactly with DMRG, and so would make a far better reference.
- Only a couple of sentences are given in the main text (not in the methods section) to describe the algorithm, and this is rather opaque. The methods section is good for describing the technical details, but given that the algorithm itself is the main novelty of the approach and major scientific advance, I would hope for a little more in the main text to describe it qualitatively.
- Furthermore, it would be good to have more insights into the convergence of the algorithm, especially in tricky cases. For instance, this is a quasi-randomized greedy optimization for a non-convex optimization problem (characterized as ‘partial-but-exact’ in the main text, which I found particularly uninformative!), so presumably there are cases where it finds local minima, exhibits a slow-down in convergence, or is found particularly sensitive to the initial conditions (perhaps e.g. where there are low-lying excited states?). It would be good to include some further insights into the numerical performance of the algorithm beyond Fig. B1, also commenting on the rate of convergence for different cases and starting point (e.g. keep the same random rotations, but reorder the initial orbitals?). How does this also vary with system size? Where is this algorithm expected to struggle to optimize to the true solutions compared to alternate iterative methods – are there any insights here?
- It would be good to compare the approach to modern approaches to (generalized) non-orthogonal CI, or fragment-localized optimization algorithms.
- There are a few minor typographical errors and inconsistent notation (e.g., missing or mismatched parentheses and indices) remain in the text—careful proofreading is advised.
Overall, the manuscript introduces an interesting and innovative algorithm for optimizing NOCI expansions. However, it does not clearly demonstrate, either numerically or a theoretical path, towards how the approach can be extended to larger systems or achieve higher accuracy (either in absolute terms or as a function of wall time) compared to existing alternatives. I would be pleased to see this work published in Nature Communications if these points can be addressed. Specifically, a more thorough and candid assessment of the algorithm’s scaling with system size is needed, both in terms of computational cost and accuracy with respect to number of determinants. This will help clarify the potential niche and practical applicability of this method, and justify its relevance for publication in a broad-interest scientific journal.

### Reviewer 3

The concept of releasing the orthogonality restrictions to obtain more compact wave functions is a very attractive one and has received quite some attention over the last decade. In the here presented manuscript, a method is described that efficiently optimizes a wave function expressed as a linear combination of non-orthogonal Slater determinants. The method has the potential to be ground-breaking and the article can become a landmark paper in the field. There are a few things that need to be looked at to put the paper in the context of previous work (point 1); to discuss the stability of the algorithm when larger, more realistic systems are targeted (point 2); to get a feeling of how important non-orthogonality is (point 3); to address the importance of full orbital relaxation (point 4) and to clarify the way in which the orbitals are picked for optimization (point 5).
1. A comparison with the work of Olsen is in place (JCP 143, 114102). In this study (and some follow-up papers) a procedure is described in which the wave function is optimized with respect to both the CI and orbital coefficients in which the configuration state functions are expressed in non-orthogonal orbitals.
2. The use of iterative solvers seems to be an unavoidable step to surpass the memory bottleneck. Although not further worked out in the manuscript, this can be a critical step in the further development of the method and make it capable to use for other than the model molecules discussed here. With the increased number of degrees of freedoms due to the loss of orthogonality and the possible linear dependencies, the use of iterative solvers may degradate the stability of the optimization process. More information on the prospects of iterative solvers could be very helpful for other researchers in the field to judge the suitability of further developing this promising method.
3. What is the degree of non-orthogonality among the different determinants? Maximum overlap, percentage of (nearly) orthogonal determinants, to name a few indicators. An overview of some numerics on this point is more than welcome.
4. The method minimizes the average energy of the wave function expressed as a linear combination of non-orthogonal Slater Determinants. This is different than the approaches that adopt a "different orbitals for different electronic configurations" strategy. The latter includes full orbital relaxation for each electronic configuration (configuration state function, Slater determinant) in the wave function, while the here presented EIDOS variant only partially recovers orbital relaxation. This is especially relevant for core-hole states or for electronic states where charge transfer excitations contribute considerably to the wave function. In such cases a much larger number of SD will be needed to obtain a balanced description of the different configurations. Is is possible to design a strategy to perform independent optimizations of the most important electronic configurations and subsequently account for the interaction between these fully relaxed (non-orthogonal) states?
5. What is the reason to randomly select the orbital that is singled out for optimization? Does this imply special advantages compared to a simple linear selection procedure? How can we be sure that all orbitals in the SD are at least optimized once? Isn't this procedure prone to get stuck in a local minimum? Furthermore, it is not at all clear how steep will be the increase in the number of iterations in this loop when bigger systems (with much more occupied orbitals) are studied.
